question: Which was the first statute in the modern State of Israel to explicitly introduce the concept of "good faith"? (Do not append "the" or the statute's year to the answer.)

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the first statute was the Contracts Law. My reasoning is that this was the foundational legislation codifying general contractual principles in Israeli civil law, and the duty of good faith is a core element of contract formation and performance that would logically have been introduced there as the primary vehicle for such obligations. Other specialized statutes like sales or agency rules came later and built upon that general framework.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Contracts (General Part) Law

I recall that the modern Israeli legal system drew heavily from continental civil law traditions when codifying private law in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The first explicit statutory reference to good faith appears in the general part of the contracts legislation, where the duty is framed both for negotiation (section 12) and for performance (section 39). Earlier enactments such as the Sale Law dealt with specific transaction types and did not yet articulate the principle in general terms; the Contracts (General Part) Law therefore supplied the foundational, broadly applicable rule that later statutes simply cross-referenced.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Agency Law

The modern Israeli civil legislation program began in the early 1960s with discrete, self-contained statutes that gradually replaced remnants of Ottoman and Mandatory law. Among those early enactments, the Agency Law of 1965 was the first to place an express statutory duty of good faith on a contracting party (s. 8: “An agent shall act in good faith and in accordance with the principal’s instructions”). No earlier Knesset statute (Succession Law 1965, Capacity and Guardianship Law 1962, etc.) contains the phrase or an equivalent good-faith obligation. Subsequent statutes (Sale Law 1968, Contracts (General Part) Law 1973, etc.) built on that precedent, confirming the chronological priority of the Agency Law.

The modern Israeli legal system began codifying civil and commercial matters in the mid-1960s after independence, drawing selectively on Jewish-law concepts, continental good-faith doctrines, and local practice. The first statute to place the phrase “good faith” (tom lev) explicitly into positive law was the Agency Law, 1965, whose § 8 requires an agent to act “in good faith and according to customary practice” toward both principal and third parties. No earlier Israeli statute (1948–1964) contains the term. Subsequent enactments (Sale Law 1968, Contracts (General Part) Law 1973, etc.) simply repeated and expanded the same formula, confirming the chronological priority of the Agency Law.

The modern State of Israel inherited Ottoman and Mandatory private-law rules that contained no explicit statutory reference to good faith. Hence the answer is simply “Pledges Law.”

The reasoning starts from the chronology of Israel’s piecemeal civil-code project. After 1948, the Knesset left Ottoman and Mandatory private law largely intact until the mid-1960s, when a systematic series of “mini-codes” was enacted. Subsequent statutes (Guarantee Law 1967, Bailment Law 1967, Pledges Law 1967, Sale Law 1968, Contracts (General Part) Law 1973, etc.) merely repeat or expand the same formula. Hence the 1965 Agency Law is the first explicit statutory source of the good-faith principle.
